parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Start by picturing two small, point-like masses in space - in which direction do they pull on each other and along what line?
Hint 2: Now think about how the size of that pull depends on the two masses and on their separation - what is multiplied and what is divided by distance squared?
parts.proper_answer: The gravitational force between two point masses is proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation, acting along the line joining their centres: $F = Gm_1m_2/r^2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture Two Point Masses Pulling Together**
You are thinking about gravity at its simplest. Treat each object as a point mass concentrated at its centre. Gravity is always attractive, so each mass pulls the other directly toward itself along the straight line joining the two centres. That direction part is essential for full credit.

Step 2: **State The Product and Inverse-Square Rule**
The size of the force grows if either mass grows, so $$F \propto m_1 m_2$$ It falls off quickly with distance, following an inverse-square law: $$F \propto \frac{1}{r^2}$$ Together with the gravitational constant $G$, this gives $$F = \frac{Gm_1 m_2}{r^2}$$ where $r$ is the separation of the centres.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: A geostationary satellite orbits the Earth. The orbit of the satellite is circular and the period of the orbit is 24 hours.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State two other features of this orbit.
hints: Hint 1: For the satellite to stay fixed over one spot on the spinning Earth, over which line of latitude must its circular path always lie?
Hint 2: Think about the way the Earth itself spins when viewed from above the North Pole - which compass direction must the satellite travel to keep up with a point on the ground?
parts.proper_answer: 1. Orbit is in the plane of the equator / directly above the equator. 2. Orbit is from west to east, in the same rotational sense as the Earth.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Stay Over The Same Point**
Geostationary means the satellite appears fixed in the sky to an observer on the ground. That can only happen if it circles around the same axis as the Earth spins. So its orbit must be centred on the Earth's centre and lie in the plane of the equator, staying directly above the equator all the time.

Step 2: **Move With The Earth**
The Earth rotates from west to east. To follow a ground station, the satellite must travel in the same direction, west to east, with the same 24 hour period. If it went east to west or over the poles, it would drift across the sky and would not be geostationary.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text:
The radius of the orbit of the satellite is $4.23 \times 10^4 \text{km}$.

Determine a value for the mass of the Earth. Explain your working.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what keeps the satellite moving in a circle at constant speed - which force supplies the required inward force?
Hint 2: Write the inward force for circular motion using orbital radius $r$ and period $T$, remembering $\omega = 2\pi/T$ and checking that $r$ is in metres and $T$ is in seconds.
Hint 3: Equate the gravitational pull $GM/r^2$ to the circular-motion requirement and rearrange algebraically to make Earth mass $M$ the subject.
Hint 4: Substitute $r = 4.23 \times 10^7 \text{ m}$, $T = 24 \text{ h} = 86400 \text{ s}$ and $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2 \text{ kg}^{-2}$ to calculate $M$.
parts.proper_answer: Gravitational force provides centripetal force: $GM/r^2 = r(2\pi/T)^2$, giving $M = 4\pi^2 r^3/(GT^2) = 6.0 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Identify Gravity As The Centripetal Force**
A satellite in steady circular orbit needs a constant inward force. There is no engine pushing it round - that inward force is the Earth's gravitational pull. So you can write: $$\text{gravitational field strength} \times \text{satellite mass} = \text{mass} \times \text{centripetal acceleration}$$ The satellite mass cancels, leaving: $$\frac{GM}{r^2} = r\omega^2$$ where $M$ is Earth mass, $r$ is orbital radius and $\omega$ is angular speed.

Step 2: **Link Angular Speed To Period**
One full orbit is angle $2\pi$ in time $T$, so $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ Substituting gives the key orbit equation: $$\frac{GM}{r^2} = r\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2$$ Rearranged for $M$: $$M = \frac{4\pi^2 r^3}{GT^2}$$

Step 3: **Convert Units Carefully**
Convert before you calculate. A very common slip is to leave $r$ in km and $T$ in hours: $$r = 4.23 \times 10^4 \text{ km} = 4.23 \times 10^7 \text{ m}$$ $$T = 24 \text{ h} = 24 \times 3600 \text{ s} = 86400 \text{ s}$$

Step 4: **Calculate The Mass Of The Earth**
Substitute $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2 \text{ kg}^{-2}$: $$M = \frac{4\pi^2 (4.23 \times 10^7)^3}{(6.67 \times 10^{-11})(86400)^2}$$ $$M \approx 6.0 \times 10^{24} \text{ kg}$$ This is the standard accepted mass of the Earth to 2 significant figures.
